headline: Netanyahu says 'no compelling evidence', calls it a 'coordinated smear campaign', contradicting the IDF
dek: Seven masked settlers attacked a diplomatic delegation in Taybeh: vehicles of France, Belgium, Poland attacked (stones, smashed window); 78-year-old French mayor Bernard Baudoux thrown to the ground, kicked, beaten with iron bars (head wound, stitches); an older woman in her 70s also beaten; 70+…
sources: Times of Israel (2 reports), SCMP, Reuters footage (Amit Orfali screengrab), Belgian FM Maxime Prevot, French mayor Bernard Baudoux (AFP/Reuters interviews), Haaretz, Netanyahu PMO statement (X), Israeli police
fault_line: Settler violence or Jewish terrorism — and does Netanyahu deny it because he needs the far right for the Oct 27 election?

sections.what_happened: On Saturday, October seventeenth, around seven masked settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation and Palestinian olive harvesters in Taybeh, near Ramallah. Vehicles belonging to the French, Belgian and Polish delegations were attacked with stones, and a Belgian consular vehicle had a window smashed. Seventy-eight-year-old French mayor Bernard Baudoux was thrown to the ground, kicked and beaten with iron bars, suffering a head wound that required stitches. An older woman in her seventies was also beaten. More than seventy sacks of harvested olives were stolen. Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot confirmed that the consul general was among those targeted, demanded an end to settler impunity, and said Belgium will press for European Union sanctions.
sections.what_verified: The attack itself is confirmed by multiple independent sources: Reuters footage of the scene, two Times of Israel reports, the South China Morning Post, Haaretz, and the French mayor's own account given to AFP and Reuters. The Israeli military itself condemned what it called a severe attack. The Belgian foreign minister's statement confirms the diplomatic personnel who were targeted. Israeli police have opened an investigation, and the military has opened a special probe.
sections.what_disputed: Prime Minister Netanyahu's office says there is no compelling evidence and called the reports a coordinated campaign to smear Israel, directly contradicting the Israeli military's own condemnation. Haaretz reports the military operations room received threat reports at one in the afternoon and did nothing until three. The exact sequence of events remains under police investigation, and no attacker has been arrested or identified. Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, who is challenging Netanyahu in the October twenty-seventh election, called the attack Jewish terrorism.
sections.why_matters: European diplomats beaten with iron bars is not a local policing story. It is a foreign policy crisis. Belgium is pushing for European Union sanctions against violent settlers, and France has a seventy-eight-year-old elected mayor with stitches in his head. The incident lands ten days before Israel's election, with the prime minister publicly at war with his own army over the facts: the military calls it a severe attack while the prime minister's office calls it a smear. That split, between the security establishment and the political leadership, is the story beneath the story.
sections.context: Taybeh is a Christian Palestinian town near Ramallah, known for its olive harvest, which is now underway. Settler violence in the West Bank has surged through the war, and this is the second attack on internationals in days, after the beating of a Washington Post photographer. European governments have condemned settler violence before, but an attack on their own diplomats raises the diplomatic cost to a new level, with sanctions now formally on the table in Brussels.

totw_analysis: Strip away the communiques and what remains is simple. Seven masked men beat a seventy-eight-year-old French mayor with iron bars while diplomats watched, and the prime minister of Israel looked at the footage and said there is no compelling evidence. The Israeli army itself disagrees with him. That is the entire story in one sentence: the state's own military calls it a severe attack, and the head of the state calls it a smear campaign. Ask who benefits from the denial. Netanyahu faces an election on October twenty-seventh and governs with the far right, the political camp most closely aligned with the settler movement. Admitting that settlers beat European diplomats with iron bars ten days before a vote would be an admission his coalition cannot afford. So the denial is not really about evidence. It is about arithmetic. Notice what is not disputed. Nobody disputes that Baudoux has stitches. Nobody disputes that the Belgian consular car was smashed. Nobody disputes that seventy sacks of olives were stolen. The denial operates one level up, in the fog of who ordered what and who knew when, where investigations can run for months and conclude nothing. That is how impunity is manufactured: not by disproving the crime, but by dissolving responsibility into procedure. The honest uncertainty is real and we state it plainly. The exact sequence, who the seven men were, whether the army's two-hour delay was negligence or something worse: all under investigation, all unknown. But the shape of the event is not unknown, and the pattern is not new. When the former chief of staff of the Israeli army calls it Jewish terrorism, he is not describing a fringe. He is describing a system that produces the same outcome, year after year, with the same result: no arrests. Brussels now has to decide whether sanctions are a threat or a policy. The mayor's stitches will heal before that question is answered.
